HELLO. WE’RE CARDISTRY.

Built around
the human moment.

The handshake. The good conversation. The “let’s work together”. That’s what a business card is really for.

Cardistry brings thoughtful print and direct-data technology together to make that moment easier. A card should look like your brand, feel considered and do its job without unnecessary complications.

Our approach is straightforward: custom PVC cards, NFC when you want it, and an optional contact QR. No mandatory hosted profile. No monthly subscription for direct-data sharing.

OUR PHILOSOPHY

Keep the card.
Lose the complications.
Design with intention.

A clear hierarchy and a distinct identity make a small card work harder. We leave room for the information that matters.

Technology with a purpose.

Direct-data sharing is a deliberate choice, not a universal compatibility claim. We explain both the benefits and the limits.

A more reusable introduction.

An NFC card can be kept and used for repeated introductions, reducing the need to hand out a new paper card each time.

THE ART OF A BETTER INTRODUCTION

What makes an NFC card genuinely offline?

Practical advice for making your next introduction a little simpler.

← All articles

“NFC” describes the way a card communicates at close range. It doesn’t, on its own, tell you whether the next step needs the internet.

The difference is in the payload.

A chip can store a website address. Tap it, and a compatible phone opens a profile page. That is convenient, but loading the profile usually depends on connectivity and the service hosting it.

A direct-data card instead stores the contact information itself in a suitable record format. A compatible reader can interpret those details locally, without fetching them from a website.

Offline doesn’t mean universal.

Phone hardware, operating systems, record types and reader apps all matter. In particular, native background NFC behaviour on iPhones does not treat arbitrary contact records the same way it treats supported web links. Some direct-data workflows may require a compatible reader app.

Ask for a test on the devices your customers actually use. An optional direct-data contact QR offers another reading route, but scanner support still needs to be checked.

What changes when your details change?

You cannot update a direct-data card by editing a hosted profile. An unlocked, writable chip can be rewritten with suitable tools, within its storage limits. A printed QR needs reprinting. If remote updates are your priority, that trade-off should be part of your decision.

A simpler relationship.

Cardistry’s direct-data model has no monthly profile subscription. The card is a tool for your next conversation, not a reason to add another recurring service.

THE ART OF A BETTER INTRODUCTION

NFC or QR? You don’t have to choose.

Practical advice for making your next introduction a little simpler.

← All articles

One uses proximity. The other uses a camera. Both can carry the same kind of introduction—if they hold the data rather than a link.

Tap: contact information on the chip.

NFC enables a compatible reader to access information at close range. Reading a direct contact record depends on the phone and software, so test the complete experience before choosing it for your audience.

Scan: contact information in the pattern.

A direct-data QR encodes the actual contact fields in its pattern. A compatible scanner can decode those fields without visiting a website. A QR containing only a URL is different: the linked page still needs connectivity.

Give your QR some breathing room.

More data can mean a denser code. Keep contact fields focused, preserve a clear quiet zone and use strong contrast. Test the final printed size on real phones rather than relying only on a large on-screen preview.

Two routes, one considered card.

Add an optional contact QR alongside NFC when you want a camera-based alternative. Neither route is a blanket guarantee for every device. The best choice is the one tested against the way your audience actually shares contacts.

THE ART OF A BETTER INTRODUCTION

Before you print: your artwork checklist.

Practical advice for making your next introduction a little simpler.

← All articles

A business card has very little space to do a lot of work. A clear brief and careful proof check make all the difference.

1. Start with the essentials.

Confirm names, job titles, company spelling, email addresses and phone numbers. Decide which details belong in the print and which should be encoded digitally. Only include information you intend to share.

2. Use your best brand files.

Provide a vector logo where possible. Avoid low-resolution screenshots. Ask Cardistry for the exact dimensions, bleed, safe area and colour requirements before preparing final exports.

3. Choose your sides deliberately.

Single-sided print works well for a focused identity. Double-sided print can separate the brand statement from practical contact information. Neither route needs to become a wall of text.

4. Treat QR as functional artwork.

Keep its background clear, preserve the quiet zone and check the actual-size printed result with multiple scanners. A decorative QR that cannot be scanned is simply a very complicated square.

5. Proof the data, not just the design.

Check every visible character and every encoded field. Confirm the NFC format on intended devices, and make sure a contact QR contains your information rather than an unintended URL. Approve the final proof before production.
